translationRepairs: In Daoguang 11 the eldest imperial son Yizhu died; he was ordered mourned by imperial-son precedent.
In Daoguang 11 the eldest imperial son Yiwei died; he was ordered mourned by imperial-son precedent.
Chinese 奕緯 is Yiwei; Yizhu (奕詝) is a different imperial son (later Xianfeng).
In Daoguang 7 the consort of the eldest imperial son Yizhu, of the Guwalgiya clan, died; inner and outer assembly and the preliminary escort to the temporary resting place were discontinued.
In Daoguang 7 the consort of the eldest imperial son Yiwei, of the Guwalgiya clan, died; inner and outer assembly and the preliminary escort to the temporary resting place were discontinued.
Same misidentification of 奕緯 as Yizhu; should be Yiwei.

In the ninth year it was fixed that for death from prince of the blood to auxiliary state duke, establishment officials wore mourning; for the twelve branches—Su, Chengze, Jingjin, Raoyu, Zheng, Keqin, Kexi, Jingning, Guermahong, Fulehei, and the like—all apportioned to a branch wore full mourning themselves and as establishment officials and titled ladies; other branches assembling removed cap tassels, retainers following their masters, senior kin without mourning.

In the ninth year it was fixed that for death from prince of the blood to auxiliary state duke, establishment officials wore mourning; for the twelve branches—Prince Li, Prince Su, Prince Chengze, Prince Jingjin, Prince Raoyu, Prince Zheng, Prince Keqin, Beile Kexi, Beile Jingning, Beizi Guermahong, and Gong Fulehei—all apportioned to a branch wore full mourning themselves and as establishment officials and titled ladies; other branches assembling removed cap tassels, retainers following their masters, senior kin without mourning.
Idiomatic omits 禮親王 (Prince Li) and compresses titled names; Chinese lists 禮親王 through 福勒黑公 explicitly.

Mourning rites for Prince Chunxian and his consort: in Guangxu 16 Prince Chun Yi died; his title was fixed as "the Emperor's biological father"; the emperor mourned one year, wore plain white eleven days, and suspended court likewise.

Mourning rites for Prince Chunxian and his consort: in Guangxu 16 Prince Chun Yiye died; his title was fixed as "the Emperor's biological father"; the emperor mourned one year, wore plain white eleven days, and suspended court likewise.
English "Prince Chun Yi" truncates 奕枻; complete personal-name romanization is Yiye.
Outer-domain condolence: in Shunzhi 13 when Mongol princes died, an official carried sacrificial text to the tomb to proclaim and sacrifice; the chief mourner led dependents to kneel and welcome.

Outer-domain condolence: in Shunzhi 13 when Mongol princes died, an official was sent bearing sacrificial text to the tomb to proclaim and sacrifice; the chief mourner led dependents to kneel and welcome.
Chinese has corrupted ★ before 祭文; sense is 賫/齎 (carry/bear) the sacrificial text, which the idiomatic already approximates but should stay aligned after character repair.

Condolence in the outer domains: in the thirteenth year of Shunzhi it was fixed that when Mongol domain princes and the like died, an official was dispatched carrying sacrificial text to the burial place to proclaim and sacrifice; the chief mourner led dependents to kneel and welcome.

Condolence in the outer domains: in the thirteenth year of Shunzhi it was fixed that when Mongol domain princes and the like died, an official was dispatched bearing the sacrificial text to the burial place to proclaim and sacrifice; the chief mourner led dependents to kneel and welcome.
Source character ★ is corruption of 賫/齎; literal should reflect bearing the text.
The next day minor encoffining: an encoffining bed east of the hall, additional garments—fifth rank and above five sets, three lined and two unlined;
The next day minor encoffining: an encoffining bed east of the hall, additional garments—third rank and above five sets, three lined and two unlined;
Chinese 三品以上 means third rank and above; literal wrongly says fifth rank.
In Qianlong 40 Qianlong specially approved that an only son might bear two sacrificial lines, fixing the precedent for dual-line succession.
In the fortieth year of Qianlong the Gaozong specially approved by edict that an only son might bear two sacrificial lines, fixing the precedent for dual-line succession.
Chinese 高宗 is the emperor's temple name; the idiomatic English repeats Qianlong for that person and drops Gaozong.
Since one-year term still used xiao gong, the dual-line son's mourning for the dual-line concubine mother was likewise.
Since the term was reduced to one year yet xiao gong was worn, the dual-line concubine mother's mourning for the dual-line son was likewise.
Chinese 兼祧庶母為兼祧子持服 means the dual-line concubine mother wore mourning for the dual-line son; the idiomatic reverses subject and object.
